abstract: This paper introduces the concept of the 'post-truth space' — clusters of densely interlinked web pages and public social media accounts that are difficult to verify or known to spread disinformation — as a tool for helping fact-checkers locate influential problematic sources. The authors situate this concept alongside four related phenomena (alternative influence networks, fake news engagement spaces, coordinated inauthentic behavior campaigns, and participatory propaganda) and develop a mapping technique combining network analysis, digital investigation of source provenance, and an influence metric. They demonstrate the method through a case study of Russia-Ukraine war discourse on Moldovan Facebook. The work was conducted as part of the EU-funded vera.ai project aimed at aiding verification specialists.
key_claims: The 'post-truth space' is a distinct and useful conceptual category among online spaces where problematic information circulates, defined as clusters of interlinked pages/accounts that are hard to verify or known disinformation sources advancing a program to assert political influence.

Post-truth spaces can be located and measured practically through a combination of mapping (inter-referencing/co-sharing of URLs), digital investigation of source provenance, and an influence metric based on cluster proximity to mainstream spaces.
The influence of a post-truth space can be gauged by its overlap with, proximity to, or penetration into more mainstream clusters; intermingling of fringe and mainstream content indicates impact.

In the Moldova case, post-truth clusters themselves had limited direct centrality, but a proximate 'borderline' content cluster (with pro-Russian material) was the most influential in the overall network and linked to the post-truth spaces.
The methods produce actionable leads for fact-checkers, who can add identified sources to curated monitoring lists.
methods: Conceptual situating of the post-truth space against four prior frameworks: alternative influence networks (YouTube co-host/co-occurrence analysis), fake news engagement spaces (engagement comparison of hyper-partisan vs. mainstream sources), coordinated inauthentic behavior (signals/signature and network analysis of synchronized sharing), and participatory propaganda (analysis of narratives, memes, and actor provenance).

Post-truth space mapping technique: querying war-related keywords in CrowdTangle (Facebook data source) to retrieve posts, accounts, pages, and groups; tidying data by shortening URLs to domains and resolving Facebook native links.

Network analysis in Gephi using the ForceAtlas2 spatialization algorithm and Louvain modularity community detection (weighted in-degree 5–50, gravity 0.005, edge weight 0.47) plus visual network analysis to identify clusters.

Digital investigation / verification techniques using Facebook transparency indicators (account name history, default 'digital creator' names, pending verification status) to assess source provenance.
A cluster betweenness centrality metric developed as a proxy for influence, measuring the extent to which post-truth clusters bridge into other communities.
Case study of Russia-Ukraine war discourse on Moldovan Facebook (mapping dated March 2023), chosen for Moldova's exposure to pro-Kremlin disinformation and Facebook's dominance there.
findings: The mapping surfaced distinct clusters in the Moldovan Facebook war discourse: three proximate 'post-truth' clusters, a 'borderline' cluster, plus conservative/nationalist, pro-Ukraine, mainstream media, and finance/military analysis clusters.

Top post-truth nodes included stiripesurse.ro (an 'alternative media' site denying the Bucha massacre), digital creator Liliana Mitrea (>17,000 followers, resharing East-West divide commentary), and Ionel Mojoiu (<10,000 followers, laundering Russian news sources like TASS, lenta.ru without attribution).
Post-truth clusters had low betweenness (Stiri pe surse 76.39, Mitrea 12.73, Mojoiu 11.14), indicating minimal direct centrality, but they supplied bridges to the influential borderline cluster.

The borderline cluster (top node Aktual24.ro, listed by Romanian cyber security as a disinformation provider) had the highest betweenness (2567.10), higher than the mainstream media cluster (Libertatea.ro, 1798.77), indicating that war discourse was driven substantially by content straddling the post-truth spaces rather than by mainstream media.
Post-truth cluster URLs were rarely shared outside their own clusters except for bridges to the borderline cluster, illustrating how the influence metric captures cluster interpenetration.
contributions: A conceptual contribution: defining and situating the 'post-truth space' among existing frameworks for studying problematic online information.

A methodological contribution: an integrated mapping technique combining keyword-based network mapping, provenance verification via platform transparency signals, and a cluster-betweenness influence metric.
A practical contribution: a workflow that generates monitorable source leads for fact-checkers and verification specialists, developed within the EU vera.ai project.
A demonstrated, replicable case-study protocol (Moldova) that can be extended to other Eastern European countries and regions.
framing: The paper positions itself within misinformation/disinformation and digital methods research, engaging debates on 'problematic information' and the post-truth phenomenon (McIntyre, Wight, Oxford Dictionaries) and building on prior typologies of online manipulation (Lewis's alternative influence networks, Silverman's fake news, Facebook's coordinated inauthentic behavior, and Wanless/Berk/Starbird's participatory propaganda). It is explicitly applied and interventionist, framed as service to fact-checking and verification practice.
